catalog_locator: Ch.1 sec. 1.5.2.1 'Tonic Prominence', pp.24-27 with fn.22 (p.27); tone inventory sec. 1.5.2 p.20 fn.17 and sec. 6.1.1 p.298; restatement sec. 6.1.2 p.299 and p.282.
catalog_quote: Unlike English, such shifting of the tonic prominence to indicate emphasis or contrast is not possible in Mizo; the tonic prominence cannot be relocated to certain parts in the clause for indicating a change in information focus. ... One main difference on comparing the examples from both the languages is that while the shift in tonic prominence is possible in English to suit the context, the tonic is always on the last syllable of the tone group in Mizo. ... During analysis, it was observed that the most prominent pitch change was always on the last syllable [fn.22] of the clause. The tonic syllable, i.e. the final syllable in the tone group, exhibited changes in intensity, duration and pitch. It always has a higher pitch or longer duration, or in the case of some attitudes, the tone completely changes or is more prominently pronounced. [fn.22] This is not just in the case of contextualized examples of Chapter 4. Even in the drama (continuous speech) text, we find the tonic prominence always on the last syllable of a tone group (see examples in Chapter 5).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mizo is a four-tone language; the only prominence the source describes is phrasal: the tonic (nuclear) prominence falls on the final syllable of the tone group/clause and cannot be moved for focus or contrast (emphasis is expressed by added pronouns, adverbs or negation instead). No word-level stress rule is given.
new_statements.exceptions: p.298: tonic prominence is never allocated to negation elements, but 'in the case of adverbials, sometimes, the adverbials are selected for tonic prominence'.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone group / clause (Hallidayan intonation unit), established instrumentally (Praat) on contextualised clauses and a continuous drama text; not a statement about the citation-form word. The only work addressing word-level stress directly (Ramdinmawii & Nath 2022, paywalled) reports in its abstract that H-tone syllables of disyllables are 'generally stressed' without a positional rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Laltleipuii 2018 describes standard Mizo (Lusei/Duhlian ṭawng) as spoken in Aizawl-area informants (EFLU study); Chhangte 1989 describes the Southern Duhlian dialect of Lunglei; Lorrain & Savidge 1898 the 'Dulien dialect'. All are lush1249. Soppitt 1887's accent rules belong to Rangkhol/Hrangkhol (hran1239), not Mizo.

tone_statements.citation: Lalhminghlui, Wendy & Priyankoo Sarmah. 2025. Acoustic Correlates of Mizo Tones. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 55(3): 503-536. doi:10.1017/S0025100325100716
tone_statements.quote: In the current study, we report four contrasting tones in Mizo, concurring with most of the previous studies (Chhangte 1993, Fanai 1992, Sarmah & Wiltshire 2010b). … As far as tone contours are concerned, we noticed that the high tone is the only level tone in Mizo, which can be represented as 33, in terms of the Chao tone numerals. The rising tone in Mizo has a falling-rising f0 pattern that is represented in terms of the Chao numerals as 213. … The low and the falling tones are represented as 21 and 31, respectively, in terms of the Chao tone numerals.
tone_statements.summary: Four contrastive tones: high (the only level tone, 33), low 21, falling 31, rising 213 (dipping); f0 slope separates them; TBU is vowel plus sonorant coda; rising-tone sandhi noted from earlier work.

tone_statements.quote: A later study by [16] conducted with a Visi-Pitch meter, finds that there are two level tones High (H) and Low (L) and two contour tones Falling (F) and Rising (R). The L mentioned by [16] is a low level tone in the underlying form, but can surface as a mid or a low level tone. [16] also separates the L tones of derived words with a glottal stop in the coda from the L tone of non-derived words, as they consistently surface as an extra low tone. … The material consisted of disyllabic (σ1σ2) compound words of all possible combinations for the four tones; Falling, High, Low and Rising.

tone_statements.summary: Four lexical tones, two level (high, low) and two contour (falling, rising), one per syllable; low may surface as mid; rising becomes low before a high-onset tone. F0 of 3 speakers classified by ANN.

tone_statements.citation: Sarmah, Priyankoo & Caroline Wiltshire. 2006. An acoustic study of Mizo tones and morpho-tonology. Abstract, 39th International Conference on Sino-Tibetan Languages and Linguistics (ICSTLL 39), University of Washington, Seattle, September 2006. 1 p.
tone_statements.quote: We confirm the findings of previous researchers by showing that Mizo has four distinct tones in the system, and show that these can be differentiated by two measures of pitch. The average F0 across the tone bearing unit (TBU=vowel plus voiced coda) relative to that of the preceding word in the frame sentence distinguishes between the H and L tones. Within a syllable with a contour tone, the pitch difference between the first and last F0s of the TBU can distinguish a rising tone from falling.
tone_statements.locator: abstract paragraph 3; tone inventory also paragraph 1 ('four tones: High, Low, Rising (=LH) and Falling (=HL)')
tone_statements.summary: Four lexical tones: High, Low, Rising (LH), Falling (HL); TBU = vowel plus voiced coda; tonal alternations under suffixation and compounding.
